TSP solution methods

Michael Hahsler and Kurt Hornik

Source: vignettes/solution_methods.Rmd
solution_methods.Rmd

This vignette uses the R package TSP (Hahsler and Hornik 2007). Please cite the package and the accompanying Journal of Statistical Software paper (see citation("TSP")) when you use it in your work.

Finding the shortest tour is NP-hard, so the number of tours that would have to be checked for an exact solution grows factorially with the number of cities. For this reason, TSP offers fast heuristics that find good (but not necessarily optimal) tours and an interface to the exact solver Concorde. This vignette describes the implemented methods and shows how to choose and compare them. All methods are called through the same function:

solve_TSP(x, method, control, ...)

where x is a TSP, ATSP or ETSP problem, method selects the algorithm, and additional arguments (or the list control) set method-specific parameters. The result is a TOUR object. See ?solve_TSP for the complete list of parameters.

Overview of the methods

Method argument Algorithm Type Problems Control parameters
"identity", "random" Order in the data / random order construction TSP, ATSP rep, two_opt, verbose
"nn" Nearest neighbor construction TSP, ATSP start, rep, two_opt, verbose
"repetitive_nn" Nearest neighbor from every start city construction TSP, ATSP two_opt, verbose
"nearest_insertion" Nearest insertion construction TSP, ATSP start, rep, two_opt, verbose
"farthest_insertion" Farthest insertion construction TSP, ATSP start, rep, two_opt, verbose
"cheapest_insertion" Cheapest insertion construction TSP, ATSP start, rep, two_opt, verbose
"arbitrary_insertion" Arbitrary insertion construction TSP, ATSP start, rep, two_opt, verbose
"two_opt" 2-opt exchange improvement TSP, ATSP tour, two_opt_repetitions, rep, two_opt, verbose
"sa" Simulated annealing improvement TSP, ATSP tour, local_move, temp, tmax, maxit, trace, rep, two_opt, verbose
"concorde" Concorde (exact, branch-and-cut) external solver TSP, ETSP clo, precision, keep_files, verbose, seed
"linkern" Chained Lin-Kernighan external solver TSP, ETSP clo, precision, keep_files, verbose, seed

Most heuristics accept the following common control parameters:

  • rep: the number of random restarts. The best tour found is returned.
  • two_opt: if TRUE, the constructed tour is refined by 2-opt improvement.
  • start: the first city for nearest neighbor and insertion algorithms.
  • verbose: show progress and the parameters that are used.

If no method is given, solve_TSP() uses arbitrary insertion followed by 2-opt improvement. Construction heuristics build a tour from scratch, while improvement heuristics start with an existing tour (given as tour) and try to shorten it. If no tour is supplied to an improvement heuristic, a random tour is used.

Tour construction heuristics

These algorithms create a tour from scratch.

Nearest neighbor

The nearest neighbor algorithm (Rosenkrantz et al. 1977) is a simple greedy procedure. It starts with a randomly chosen city (or the city given by start) and repeatedly appends the nearest city that has not been visited yet. It is very fast, but typically has to make long “jumps” at the end of the tour to reach the remaining cities.

The repetitive variant ("repetitive_nn") runs the algorithm once from every city and returns the shortest tour found.

Insertion algorithms

All insertion algorithms (Rosenkrantz et al. 1977) start with a tour consisting of a single city and repeatedly insert a city \(k\) that is not yet on the tour between two consecutive tour cities \(i\) and \(j\) so that the increase in tour length

\[d(i,k) + d(k,j) - d(i,j)\]

is minimal. They differ in how the city to be inserted is chosen:

  • Nearest insertion chooses the city closest to any city on the tour.
  • Farthest insertion chooses the city farthest from the tour. This first establishes an outline of the whole tour and fills in details later. In practice, farthest insertion often produces better tours than the other insertion variants.
  • Cheapest insertion chooses the city with the lowest insertion cost.
  • Arbitrary insertion chooses a random city. It is the fastest variant.

For distances that obey the triangle inequality, nearest and cheapest insertion are related to Prim’s minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim 1957) and guarantee tours that are at most twice the optimal length.

Tour improvement heuristics

These heuristics modify existing tours to improve them. If no starting tour is specified then typically a random tour is used as the starting point.

2-opt is very effective. Many constructive methods have for convenience the control parameter two_opt which automatically applies 2-opt improvment to the constructed tour.

2-opt

Two-opt (Croes 1958) repeatedly removes two edges from the tour and reconnects the two resulting paths in the only other possible way (which is equivalent to reversing a part of the tour) whenever this shortens the tour. The procedure stops at a 2-optimal tour, i.e., a local optimum for this neighborhood. "two_opt_repetitions" can be used to restart the algorithm from random tours.

Simulated annealing

Simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick et al. 1983) uses random local moves (reversal of a random sub-tour) and accepts moves that make the tour longer with a probability that decreases as the temperature is lowered. This allows the search to escape local optima. The implementation uses stats::optim() with method "SANN". The method is usually much slower than 2-opt and needs tuning of the cooling schedule (temp, tmax, maxit). By default, only 10,000 evaluations are used to keep the run time short, so a larger maxit is needed for competitive results.

Improving an existing tour

Improvement heuristics can be applied to any tour, including a tour that was created outside of TSP. For example, we can refine a nearest neighbor tour with 2-opt and then use a long simulated annealing run for further improvement.

library(TSP)
data(USCA50)

nn <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", start = 1)
opt2 <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "two_opt", tour = nn)
set.seed(1234)
sa <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "sa", tour = opt2, maxit = 50000)

c(nn = tour_length(nn), two_opt = tour_length(opt2), sa = tour_length(sa))
#>      nn two_opt      sa 
#>   17032   16341   15008

We see how improvement methods reduce the tour length.

State-of-the-art solvers

Concorde (Applegate et al. 2006) is currently one of the best exact solvers for symmetric TSPs. It uses the branch-and-cut method (Padberg and Rinaldi 1990) which iteratively tightens a linear programming relaxation of the problem. The Chained Lin-Kernighan heuristic (Applegate et al. 2003), an extension of the Lin-Kernighan heuristic (Lin and Kernighan 1973), is a very fast heuristic that finds excellent tours for large instances. Both are accessed via the "concorde" and "linkern" methods, but require that the Concorde executables are installed separately. See vignette("concorde") for details.

Asymmetric and Euclidean problems

All heuristics above work with asymmetric problems (ATSP). Solvers that only handle symmetric problems use an automatic reformulation as a symmetric TSP with twice as many cities (see ?reformulate_ATSP_as_TSP).

Euclidean problems (ETSP) are converted into distance matrices for the built-in heuristics, which needs memory proportional to the square of the number of cities. Only "concorde" and "linkern" work with ETSP objects directly.

Reproducibility

Many methods are randomized (e.g., "random", "nn" with a random start, "arbitrary_insertion", "sa", and all methods with rep > 1). They use R’s global random-number stream. Calling set.seed() before solve_TSP() makes a run reproducible, and every call advances the stream as any other R function that draws random numbers does.

data(USCA50)

set.seed(1234)
tour1 <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", rep = 10)
#> Warning: executing %dopar% sequentially: no parallel backend registered

set.seed(1234)
tour2 <- solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", rep = 10)

identical(as.integer(tour1), as.integer(tour2))
#> [1] TRUE

Parallel execution

Repetitions (including "repetitive_nn") are run using the foreach package and can be executed in parallel by registering a backend before calling solve_TSP().

library(doParallel)
registerDoParallel()
solve_TSP(USCA50, method = "nn", two_opt = TRUE, rep = 100)

For parallel repetitions, one random number per repetition is drawn from R’s global stream in the main R process and used to seed the iteration (on the main process or a worker). The results are therefore reproducible with set.seed() independent of the backend and the number of workers.
